Theodosius
thē-ō-dō´shĭ-ŭs
n. (Roman emperor 379–395, who made Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire and was excommunicated by Ambrose of Milan)
Greek Theodosios, gift of God. His reign closed the Arian controversy politically and opened a longer question: what happens to a church that the state has adopted.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Theodosius made orthodoxy imperial policy, and in 390 ordered a massacre at Thessalonica; Ambrose refused him communion until he did public penance, and he submitted. Scripture supplies the two halves of that story. The magistrate is God's servant: “he is the minister of God to thee for good… for he beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4), and the church is to be subject to him (Rom 13:1). And the magistrate is under a word he does not control: Nathan said to David, “Thou art the man” (2Sa 12:7). His heart is not his own: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1). And the spheres are distinguished: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines emperor as the sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; and excommunication as the act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the church.

expand to see more

EMPEROR, n. The sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; a title of dignity superior to that of king.

EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of a church, by an ecclesiastical sentence.

PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority, as a punishment for his faults.

Key Scripture

Rom 13:4 — "For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

2Sa 12:7 — "And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;"

Pro 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Mat 22:21 — "They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

Modern Corruption

State establishment is remembered as the church's victory, and it cost more than it bought.

expand to see more

The episode with Ambrose is genuinely admirable and should be told first. An emperor who could execute a bishop was refused the sacrament by one, on the ground of blood shed at Thessalonica, and he did public penance. That is a bishop exercising the only authority the church has — a spiritual one — against the greatest power on earth, and winning. It is the exact opposite of the church borrowing the sword, and it is the model the Reformed have pointed to whenever they argued that ecclesiastical and civil authority are distinct.

The longer consequence of establishment is harder to admire. When belonging to the church becomes the path to office and advantage, the church fills with people who have not been converted, discipline weakens because the members are the population, and the state acquires an interest in what is preached. Within a generation of Theodosius the imperial power was being used against heretics, and the precedent set there ran through a thousand years and reached Servetus. A church protected by the sword will eventually be asked to bless it.

The Baptist and wider Reformed answer — a regenerate membership, a distinct spiritual authority, liberty of conscience under a magistrate who has no jurisdiction over the soul — is an answer to this history. It does not despise the magistrate; Romans 13 is unambiguous, and a Christian owes subjection, honour and taxes to rulers far worse than Theodosius. It says only that Caesar's things and God's things are different things, that Christ said so, and that the church loses more than it gains whenever it forgets which it is holding.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek exousiai huperechousai (G1849), the higher powers; diakonos theou (G1249), the minister of God; machaira (G3162), the sword; apodote (G591), render.

expand to see more

Greek diakonos theou (G1249) — God's minister, said of the civil magistrate; Romans 13:4 twice.

Greek machaira (G3162) — sword; Romans 13:4 — committed to the magistrate, never to the church.

Greek apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari (G591) — render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's; Matthew 22:21, Mark 12:17, Luke 20:25.

Usage

"“He beareth not the sword in vain” — and the sword is the magistrate's."

"“Thou art the man” — a prophet, to a king, with no army."

"“Unto Caesar… and unto God” — different things."
